job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Felix Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I get up at eight, same as when I had lectures, because otherwise the day slides away. I send two or three applications through the company portals and rewrite my CV for each one. In the afternoon I do my mum's shopping or fix something on the family computer, and my younger sister Nina asks me to explain her maths homework. I graduated seven months ago in computer science, top of my year, with internships at Calder Haulage's help desk and a hospital trust's data team, and I still have no offer. That wears on me more than I let on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it to other graduates, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so to the people who swore coders were about to be replaced. Online I'd stay quiet, because I barely post. With friends I'd say the hype made companies stop hiring graduates for a year, and now the hype fades and nobody calls us back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Even if AI is hype, the hiring freeze started because of the hype, and firms don't undo that quickly. I've sent about 140 applications and had four interviews. I have roughly two months of savings and a student loan sitting there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep applying, but wider: the council, the hospital trust, the railway. I'd ask Mr Okafor, my old supervisor at the hospital trust, to give a reference call. And I'd spend evenings at the library on the networking certificate I'm missing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, mostly. Not scared exactly, but flat. It feels like waiting at a bus stop where the timetable might be wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the freeze started because of the hype. Who do you hold responsible?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big firms that cut their graduate schemes to look lean for investors. I'm not against technology, I'm against bosses using it as an excuse. A union for junior tech workers would at least give us someone to ask, and my uncle's union at the rail depot protected people in the last downturn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a good day look like in six months?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A signed contract, even a boring one, fixing databases for a water company. I'd tell my mum first, then Nina, who has been lending me bus fare. Then I'd start paying the loan properly and look for a shared flat in town.

say: I'd say the **hype** gave firms an excuse to stop hiring juniors, and the hype fading won't fix that.
I'd tell friends to **keep applying**, because the openings are thinner but still there.
think: Privately I think I'm **stuck**: the freeze outlasts the hype, and my savings only cover about two months.
I'm angry at big firms for cutting **graduate schemes** to impress investors.
do: Widen applications to **council, hospital and railway** IT teams.
Ask Mr Okafor for a **reference call** this month.
Study the missing **networking certificate** at the library in the evenings.
feel: Flat and **tired**, like waiting at a bus stop with a timetable that may be wrong.
S0.quote: Even if AI is hype, the hiring freeze started because of the hype, and firms don't undo that quickly.
fieldNote: Felix blames employers, not the technology, and wants a **union** for junior tech workers.
He sounds composed but counts savings in months, which shows the real pressure.
Never uses AI tools; he treats them as the boss's excuse, not his own problem.

steps.text: Send three tailored applications a day to council, hospital and railway IT teams
Study for the networking certificate at the library each evening
Ask Mr Okafor for a reference call and ask family for bus fare

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second picture. It's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it to other graduates, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's not a revolution, it's a slow squeeze on people like me. Writing code, checking it, testing it, those are the first things they hand to software. I'd tell friends to join a union before the squeeze gets worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Entry-level coding is exactly what gets cut first. Firms will say one senior developer plus a tool can do what three juniors did. I haven't even used the tools, so I'd be behind on top of everything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have to finally try them, which I hate. I'd spend a month learning how the tools work, mainly so I can read what they produce and spot errors. I'd also apply for jobs that check and test systems, since someone has to be accountable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy and a bit insulted. I worked hard at university to learn how things work underneath, and now that's treated as a slow way of doing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you've never tried the tools. What's holding you back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I don't trust where they get their answers, and I don't like feeding my work into some company's machine. It's also pride, because I want to understand every line I write. My lecturer said that's a good habit and a slow one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the government for in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rules that say firms must keep training juniors, and some money for firms that do. Also a clear answer on who is responsible when a tool's code breaks something. Right now nobody signs for it, and that frightens me.

say: I'd say this is a **squeeze** on junior workers and we need a union before it gets worse.
I'd tell friends that **checking and testing** code will matter more than writing it.
think: Entry-level coding goes first, and I'm **behind** because I've never used the tools.
I resent that my **understanding** of how things work is now called slow.
do: Spend a month **learning the tools**, mostly to read and test what they produce.
Apply for **testing and checking** roles where someone must sign for the result.
Write to my local representative about **training rules** for firms.
feel: Uneasy and a bit **insulted**, because careful learning now counts for less.
S1.quote: Firms will say one senior developer plus a tool can do what three juniors did.
fieldNote: Resistance is partly **pride** and partly distrust of where the tools get their answers.
He moves from blame to concrete asks: **training rules** and clear responsibility.
Reluctantly willing to try the tools once the pressure is real.

steps.text: Spend a month learning to use AI coding tools and spot their errors
Apply for software testing and checking roles at hospitals and utilities
Write to the local representative about rules to keep firms training juniors

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the third picture. It's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it to other graduates, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is a cliff. I'd tell friends this is the moment for unions, public rules and a basic income, because the market won't sort it out in time. Online I'd probably just share other people's warnings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my degree loses its worth before I even use it. If AI does any thinking job better and cheaper, nobody needs a graduate to write code. The hands-on side is safer for a few years, but I only know software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move back to my parents' for good to save rent and sit on whatever savings I have. I'd look for anything hands-on near home, perhaps working with the electricians my uncle knows, learning the trade. I'd also help my mum cut our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, honestly. It's like finishing a long race and finding the finish line has been taken down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said robots take about three more years. Does that change your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, a bit. It means a trade like electrical work gives me until about 2031, and in that time I might build something to live on. But I'd feel like I'm running from a bear that's slower than the first one, not safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your sister Nina?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my sister Nina to keep doing well at school but not to pin her life on a single career. I'd say her brother's degree might be worth less than he hoped, and that's not her fault or mine. I'd try not to scare her.

say: I'd say two years is a **cliff** and only public rules and a basic income can soften it.
I'd share warnings online and push friends towards **unions**.
think: My degree may lose its **worth** before I ever use it in a real job.
The hands-on side buys about **three years**, but I only know software.
do: Stay at my parents' and **save** every spare pound against the loan.
Ask my uncle about **electrician** work and a trade course.
Help Mum cut **household bills** by about 15 percent.
feel: **Frightened**, like finishing a race and finding the finish line gone.
S2.quote: I'd tell my sister Nina to keep doing well at school but not to pin her life on a single career.
fieldNote: Felix thinks **collectively**: unions and basic income, not personal reinvention.
The robot delay gives him a plan but not **comfort**.
He worries about his sister Nina more than about himself.

steps.text: Stay at my parents' and put every spare pound towards the student loan
Cut the family's household bills by about a sixth with Mum
Ask my uncle about electrician work and a trade course
Join the junior tech workers' union and go to the first meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fourth picture. It's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it to other graduates, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is a bit more room, but not much. I'd say what I said about two years, only with more time to organise. I'd push friends to join the union and write to local politicians while we still can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years lets me build a second skill. I could finish the networking certificate and a trade qualification in that time. The software jobs vanish around 2031, but the hands-on ones hold until about 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd land any job I can in the first year, even a help desk one, and take evening classes in electrical installation. I'd keep paying the loan down. I'd also ask Nina's school if I can run a small coding club, so I stay in practice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less frightened than the two-year picture, more worn out. It's like a long uphill walk rather than a fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which would you rather have, a help-desk job now or a trade course first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The job, because money and a reference matter. But I'd work it with an end date in my head, three years at most. I won't sit still waiting for that help desk to be automated.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in your life would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad, who is 58 and a delivery supervisor. If software plans the routes, his job shrinks first. He won't say it, but I've seen him reading about it at night.

say: I'd say five years is **room to organise**, so join the union and write to politicians now.
I'd tell friends to build a **second skill** quickly.
think: Five years lets me finish the **certificate** and a trade qualification before software jobs thin out.
I'm quietly worried about **my dad**, whose delivery-routing job could shrink first.
do: Take any **help desk job** in year one and keep paying the loan.
Run a small **coding club** at Nina's school to stay in practice.
feel: **Worn out** more than frightened, like a long uphill walk.
S3.quote: I won't sit still waiting for that help desk to be automated.
fieldNote: Felix sets an **end date** for any stopgap job, which shows planning under pressure.
His fear shifts to his **father**, a delivery supervisor reading about route software at night.
Still no wish to use AI tools unless forced.

steps.text: Take any help desk job in the first year and keep paying the loan
Join evening classes in electrical installation
Save a third of every wage until the loan is halved
Run a small coding club at Nina's school each Saturday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fifth picture. It's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it to other graduates, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is long enough to actually change my life, so I'd feel less panicky about it. I'd still say the rules need writing now, while there's time. Online I'd probably argue for retraining money for anyone who loses work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think ten years means my generation can survive it if we plan. I'd get a first job, build savings and learn a trade, maybe do a master's in something that stays human, like safety engineering. I'm mostly worried about the first two years, not the last eight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any decent job in the next six months and do a part-time course in electrical safety. I'd move into a shared flat in town by next summer. I'd also join the union branch and actually go to meetings, not just pay the fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer than the others, though not relaxed. It feels like having the weather forecast a week in advance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any part of the ten-year picture that bothers you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That people will say there's loads of time and then do nothing. My uncle's depot knew the closure was coming for years and nobody planned. I don't want to be one of the ones who knew and froze.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently from your parents' generation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep a second skill alive, and I'd keep one foot in a union. My dad never thought he'd need either. I'd also move for work earlier, rather than wait for the right job to appear in our town.

say: I'd say ten years is **enough time** if the rules for retraining are written now.
I'd argue online for **retraining money** for anyone who loses work.
think: My generation can survive it if we **plan**, and the first two years are the hard part.
I don't want to be someone who **knew and froze**, like the depot workers.
do: Take a decent job in six months and study **electrical safety** part time.
Move to a **shared flat** in town by next summer.
Go to **union meetings** instead of just paying the fee.
feel: Calmer, like having a **weather forecast** a week ahead, though not relaxed.
S4.quote: I don't want to be one of the ones who knew and froze.
fieldNote: Ten years turns his dread into a **plan**: job, savings, second skill.
He draws on his uncle's depot story: the closure was known and **nobody prepared**.
Calmest here, but the early job search still sits heavy.

steps.text: Take a decent junior IT job within six months of now
Study electrical safety part time in the evenings
Move into a shared flat in town by next summer
Go to every monthly union branch meeting

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, without a doubt. No time to plan, my degree hits the floor, and my dad's job is exposed too. What would help is rules that make firms keep training juniors, some retraining money, and a union that actually speaks for people my age.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm more stubborn than I look. People say I should just use the tools, and I know that, but I want my reasons to be mine. And I'd like someone to hire me so I can prove I'm worth it.

headlineQuote: A signed contract, even a boring one, fixing databases for a water company.
portrait: Felix is a 23-year-old **computer science** graduate, top of his year, living at home with his parents and sister Nina.
He has had seven months of job hunting, **140 applications** and four interviews, with about two months of savings and a loan.
He leans left, blames **employers** for using AI as an excuse and wants unions and public rules for junior workers.
He never uses AI tools and resists them out of **pride** and distrust, though he would try them if forced.
He worries about his sister and his **father's** delivery job, and plans a second trade as a backup.
biggestWorry: The two-year **AGI** picture worries him most, since his degree would lose its worth before he could use it.
whatWouldHelp: He wants rules making firms keep **training juniors**, retraining money, and a union that speaks for young workers.
